pipe.def: Sends the output of one command into the next, so `zcat file.gz | head -3` shows three lines of a compressed file without unpacking it.
levels: Imagine a line of toy trucks passing buckets of blocks to each other. A pipe in the terminal does that with words: whatever one command hands out, the next command catches and uses right away.

The pipe symbol `|` connects two terminal commands so the output of the first becomes the input of the second, without saving anything to a file in between. `ls | head -3` lists the files in a folder and only keeps the first three lines. This lets you chain small tools into one line instead of writing a program.

A pipe connects one process's standard output to the next process's standard input, so `command1 | command2` runs both at once, streaming data between them. `zcat file.gz | head -3` decompresses a gzipped file and immediately shows the first three lines, without ever writing an unzipped copy to disk. You can chain more than two: `cat log.txt | grep ERROR | wc -l` counts error lines in one line.

A pipe is built on the same file-descriptor mechanism as redirection, but instead of connecting a process to a file, the shell connects one process's stdout directly to another's stdin through an in-memory buffer, so both processes run concurrently rather than one waiting to finish before the next starts. Because the buffer is bounded, a slow consumer can block a fast producer, which is why streaming tools that read incrementally, like `head` or `grep`, can short-circuit a huge upstream computation, as `zcat file.gz | head -3` does: `zcat` stops decompressing once `head` has what it needs and closes the pipe. Pipes only carry bytes, so structured data crossing a pipe, JSON lines, CSV, needs both ends to agree on a text format. Failures are silent by default: an error in the first command of a pipeline does not stop the second from running on empty or partial input, unless `set -o pipefail` is set.

The concurrency that makes pipes fast also makes them a common source of subtle bugs: a pipeline's exit status is normally that of its last command, so a failure early in the chain, `grep` finds nothing, a command segfaults, can be masked unless `pipefail` is on, which is why production shell scripts set `set -euo pipefail` as a matter of course. Buffering behavior differs by program and by whether stdout is a terminal or a pipe: many tools switch from line-buffered to block-buffered output when piped, which can make `tail -f log | grep pattern` appear to hang even though data is flowing, a classic surprise fixed with `stdbuf` or a tool's own line-buffered flag. Pipes fit Unix's small-tools philosophy well for text streams, but they are a poor fit for anything needing random access or two-way communication, where a named pipe or a socket is the right tool instead. Practitioners sometimes reach for a pipeline where a single script would be clearer and more testable; the discipline is to pipe when each stage is a genuine, reusable filter, not just to avoid writing Python.

At production scale, the pipe's idea generalizes far past the shell: a batch pipeline of Parquet-to-Parquet stages, a stream processor's operator graph, and a Unix pipe are all the same pattern of composable, backpressured stages, and the same failure modes reappear, a silently swallowed error in an early stage, an unbuffered stage stalling the whole chain under load. The open engineering question at that scale is less about the pipe itself and more about observability: knowing, for a multi-stage pipeline processing millions of rows an hour, exactly which stage is slow or wrong without re-running the whole thing, which is why production systems replace bare shell pipes with orchestrators that log per-stage metrics, the way this project's own scripts print one structured line per stage.

jupyter-notebook.def: An app that runs Python one cell at a time and shows results, tables and plots under each cell. Good for looking at data; scripts are better for the pipeline.
levels: A Jupyter notebook is like a picture book where each page has a little bit of computer code, and when you tap the page, the computer does that bit and draws the answer right underneath.

A Jupyter notebook is an app that runs Python code one chunk, called a cell, at a time, instead of running a whole file at once. You type code into a cell and press shift-enter, and the result, a number, a table, or a plot, appears right under it. It is great for poking at data, but for a program that should run the same way every time, a plain `.py` script is better.

A notebook file (`.ipynb`) stores a sequence of cells, each either code or explanatory text, along with the saved output from the last time each cell ran. Running cells out of order is easy and dangerous: a variable defined in cell 5 and used in cell 2 will work in the notebook's current session but fail if you restart and run top to bottom, so 'Restart and run all' before trusting a notebook's results. For example, you might load a month of PeMS data in one cell, then run `df.describe().T` in the next to see each column's range, with the table appearing immediately below.

A notebook is a JSON file wrapping a persistent Python kernel: state, variables, imports, lives in that running kernel process, not in the file, so displayed outputs can silently drift out of sync with the code as cells are edited and rerun in a different order than they appear on the page. This makes notebooks excellent for exploratory data analysis, where you want to see a table or a plot after every small step and keep looking at real numbers rather than staring at code, but poor for anything that must be reproducible, tested, or run unattended, because hidden state and out-of-order execution are invisible in the saved file. The standard discipline is to prototype in a notebook, then move working logic into functions in a `.py` module that both the notebook and a production script import, so the two never diverge. Version control is also awkward: notebooks store output alongside code, so diffs are noisy unless outputs are stripped before committing.

The tension between notebooks and scripts is really a tension between exploratory and confirmatory analysis, and treating a notebook as a pipeline stage conflates the two: a data scientist tweaking a threshold cell by cell is doing exploration, and a scheduled job producing tomorrow's predictions needs a deterministic script with no hidden kernel state. Tools like `nbconvert`, `papermill`, and `jupytext`, which pairs a notebook with a plain-text `.py` mirror, exist precisely because teams want the interactivity during development and the reproducibility of a script in production, and getting the boundary wrong, shipping notebooks as production code, is a common and expensive mistake. A subtler failure practitioners hit constantly: a notebook that looks correct top to bottom because cells were run in a convenient order during debugging, not the order printed on the page, so a colleague's 'Restart and run all' produces a different, sometimes wrong, result. Extensions like autoreload and interactive widgets add further hidden state that can make a notebook's behavior depend on invisible history.

In research and applied teams, notebooks remain the default surface for first-look data analysis and model debugging because switching to a script for every quick question costs too much, but any result meant to be trusted, a claim in a paper, a number that drives a launch decision, gets re-derived in a script or test that runs clean from a fresh kernel before anyone relies on it. Newer tools, reactive notebooks that automatically rerun downstream cells when an upstream one changes, try to fix the hidden-state problem at the tool level rather than through discipline, and it remains an open question whether reactive execution can keep the fast, ad hoc feel that makes notebooks useful while removing their central reproducibility failure.

json.def: A text format for lists and dictionaries (`{"h": 30, "p": 0.42}`) that every language can read. Used for thresholds, feature lists and the live predictions file.
levels: JSON is a way of writing down a list of facts, like the ball is red and the ball is round, using curly braces and colons, so any computer in the world can read it and understand which fact is which.

JSON is a text format for storing structured data: numbers, strings, lists, and dictionaries, which are lookup tables from a name to a value. It looks like `{"h": 30, "p": 0.42}`, meaning h is 30 and p is 0.42. Almost every programming language can read and write JSON, which is why it is used to pass data between very different programs.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) nests four building blocks: numbers, strings in double quotes, lists in square brackets, and objects (dictionaries) in curly braces mapping string keys to values. Python's `json` module converts between JSON text and native objects: `json.dump(obj, f)` writes a dict or list to a file, and `json.load(f)` reads it back. In this course, `models/calibration.json` stores the alert threshold τ per horizon, for example `{"15": 0.62, "30": 0.51, "60": 0.44}`, so changing the required precision later means rerunning one small step, not retraining.

JSON's four data types, number, string, boolean or null, and the two containers, array and object, form a strict grammar with no comments and no trailing commas, which is what makes it unambiguous to parse in any language but also unforgiving to hand-edit. It has no native representation for dates, sets, or NaN, so a Python `datetime` or `numpy.nan` must be converted, typically to an ISO string and `null` respectively, before serialization, and `float()` is the usual fix for numpy scalars that otherwise raise a type error on serialization. It is a good format for small, structured configuration and output, thresholds, feature lists, one row of live predictions, but a poor one for millions of numeric rows, where its per-value text overhead and lack of columnar structure make Parquet far smaller and faster to read. JSON Lines, one JSON object per line, is the common middle ground for streaming many records without loading a giant array into memory at once.

JSON's simplicity is also its limitation as a schema-less format: nothing in the file itself enforces that every prediction record has the same keys or that `p` is always a float between 0 and 1, so validation has to happen in code, with libraries like `pydantic` or JSON Schema filling that gap when a service's contract must be enforced. A subtlety practitioners hit often: JSON numbers have no fixed precision, and different parsers round large integers or long floats differently, which matters for anything like a hash or a high-precision timestamp passed through JSON. In a serving system, JSON is usually the wire format for an API's request and response, readable and debuggable with `curl`, while the storage format underneath is something denser, Parquet, Avro, or a database, precisely because JSON's human-readability trades away compactness and typed schema enforcement.

At scale, JSON stays the lingua franca at system boundaries, an API response, a config file, a log line, because every tool speaks it, but internal high-throughput paths move to binary, schema'd formats, Protocol Buffers, Avro, Arrow, once record count and the need for backward-compatible schema evolution outgrow what a schema-less text format can enforce safely. The open craft problem is less about JSON itself and more about contract discipline: keeping producers and consumers of a JSON API in sync as fields are added, renamed, or deprecated, which is why schema registries and strict validation at the boundary, rather than JSON's own grammar, are what actually keep large systems from breaking on silent format drift.

station.def: One sensor site on the freeway, identified by a number. It reports flow, occupancy and speed every five minutes.
levels: A station is a little box by the side of the road that watches the cars go by and counts them, like a lookout who calls in a report every five minutes.

A station is one detector site on the freeway, and every station has its own ID number, stored in the `station_id` column. Every five minutes, a station reports how many cars passed (flow), what fraction of the time a car was over the sensor (occupancy), and how fast cars were going (speed). A single freeway has many stations, one every mile or so, each watching its own stretch of road.

In the PeMS data, a station is one physical detector, identified by a number, that logs a row every five minutes with `flow`, `occ` and `speed`, plus metadata like which freeway (`fwy`), direction (`dir`), and Caltrans district it belongs to. `df[df.station_id == 400001]`, for example, pulls out one station's rows across a month; sorting by timestamp turns that selection into a single time series, one row per five minutes, for that one physical location. Two stations right next to each other, upstream and downstream, are what later features use for neighbor information.

A station defines the spatial unit of the whole prediction problem: the task is framed as supervised classification on a panel indexed by station and time, where the feature vector for station s at time t is built only from information available at or before t, and the target is whether that same station is in a slow episode some horizon later. Because stations are physically ordered along a freeway, they are not independent units; a slowdown detected at an upstream station is informative about what a downstream station will see minutes later, which is exactly what neighbor and adjacency features exploit. Not every station reports cleanly: `pct_obs` below 50 flags rows that are mostly PeMS's own fill-in rather than real readings, and stations can have missing days, sensor faults, or coverage gaps that the cleaning stage has to handle per station, since pooling all stations' raw rows together would blur these station-specific failure patterns.

Treating station as the fixed unit of analysis is a modeling choice with real cost: it assumes station identity is meaningful and stable, but detectors get replaced, recalibrated, or renumbered, and a model trained on one set of station IDs generalizes poorly to a station added after training unless features are built from properties, freeway, direction, historical traffic pattern, rather than the raw ID as a categorical. The panel structure also creates a leakage trap that is easy to get wrong: splitting train and validation randomly across station-time rows leaks information, because nearby timestamps at the same station are highly correlated, so splits must respect time, and often station generalization, rather than shuffling rows. A further subtlety is that stations are not spaced uniformly and do not all have the same physical meaning; a mainline station and a ramp station see structurally different traffic, and lumping them together as one population without that distinction is a common source of confused feature importances.

In systems that scale past one metro's fixed loop-detector network, the station abstraction itself becomes the bottleneck: newer sensing, connected vehicles, cameras, probe-vehicle speeds, reports on road segments rather than fixed points, so production systems increasingly model a dynamic, changing graph of locations rather than a fixed roster of station IDs, and transferring a model trained on one city's stations to another city's, where station identity is meaningless, is an open research problem tackled with graph representations keyed on road geometry rather than detector number. At Fremont's own scale, the practical version of this problem is simpler but still real: handling a station going offline, being added, or being renumbered without retraining the entire model or silently dropping its neighbors from every other station's features.

pct-obs.def: The percentage of a five-minute row that came from real observations rather than PeMS's fill-in estimates. Below 50 the row is mostly guesswork.
levels: Sometimes the road counter misses and guesses instead of really counting, and `pct_obs` is a number that tells you how much of what it just said was a real count versus a guess.

`pct_obs` is a column in the PeMS data that shows what percentage of a five-minute row came from the sensor actually working, rather than PeMS filling in a guess for a gap. A value of 100 means every reading behind that row was real; a value of 20 means most of it is estimated. Rows with low `pct_obs` are less trustworthy and often get treated specially during cleaning.

Each five-minute PeMS row is built from several raw samples, and `pct_obs` records what share of those samples were actually observed versus filled in by PeMS's own imputation. The cleaning rule in this course is `day.loc[day.pct_obs < 50, ["speed", "occ", "flow"]] = np.nan`: any row where less than half the data is real gets its three measurements blanked out rather than trusted. `print(df.describe().T)` is one way to check how common low `pct_obs` rows are across a month, since sensor coverage varies a lot by station.

`pct_obs` is PeMS's own confidence signal on a five-minute aggregate, and its distribution is not uniform: it depends on detector age, weather, and maintenance schedule, so treating it as missing completely at random is usually wrong. The threshold of 50 used in this course is a judgment call, not a law of nature, chosen because below it a row is more estimate than measurement, and passing it downstream unflagged would let the model learn from PeMS's imputation algorithm rather than the road. Blanking with NaN rather than deleting the row is deliberate: it keeps the row on the regular five-minute time grid, which later lag and rolling features depend on, while any feature computed from a blanked value correctly becomes missing rather than silently wrong. A model that ignores `pct_obs` entirely risks learning spurious patterns tied to which detectors happen to have worse coverage rather than to real traffic.

The deeper issue `pct_obs` surfaces is that PeMS's own imputation is itself a model, typically some form of historical average or nearest-neighbor fill, and any downstream model trained on rows with moderate `pct_obs` partially learns to reproduce that upstream model's assumptions rather than ground truth, a subtle form of leakage from one modeling pipeline into another. Practitioners often set a single global threshold, as this course does, but a more careful treatment would let it vary by how a feature will be used: an aggregate like a daily average tolerates lower `pct_obs` than a real-time alert feature does, because averaging cancels noise a single five-minute decision cannot. It is also easy to forget that `pct_obs` describes the input row, not the label; a target computed from a low-`pct_obs` future row is itself uncertain in a way the loss function never sees unless labels below some coverage are also excluded or down-weighted.

At production scale, `pct_obs`-style provenance flags generalize into a broader discipline of tracking data quality metadata alongside every value, not just for sensor networks but for any pipeline that mixes real and imputed or synthetic data, because a model silently trained partly on a vendor's own imputation degrades in ways hard to diagnose from aggregate metrics alone. The open engineering question is less what threshold and more how to propagate uncertainty: ideally a low-`pct_obs` row would contribute a downweighted, wider-uncertainty training signal rather than a binary keep-or-blank decision, which is the kind of soft data-quality weighting production ML systems increasingly support but that adds real complexity to a training pipeline.

incident.def: A 511 event: crash, stall, closure, with created, updated and pulled-at times. Its reporting delay limits how much it can help.
levels: An incident is when something happens on the road, like a crash or a stall, and a helper called 511 writes it down with the time it happened, kind of like a hall monitor reporting that there was a spill by the door.

An incident is an event from the 511 traffic feed: a crash, a stall, a closure, or roadwork, each with a location and a time. The 511 service is polled every 15 minutes, and each incident is logged with `created` (first reported), `updated` (details changed), and `pulled_at` (when this project's own collector fetched it). Incidents are one of the two main data sources for the traffic project, alongside the five-minute detector rows from PeMS.

An incident record comes from 511.org and includes a road name, a map point, and three timestamps: `created`, `updated`, and `pulled_at`, logged by `02_collect_events.py` every time it polls the feed. Because 511 is sampled every 15 minutes rather than continuously, an incident's start and end times are interval-censored: the true crash time is somewhere before `created`, not exactly at it. An `incident_active` flag built from this feed can be joined to the five-minute detector rows as one input feature, marking every row within some distance and time window of a live incident.

Incident data carries its own measurement error layered on top of the freeway's real state: reporting delay, the gap between the physical event and CHP logging it, missing or approximate geography, unrecorded severity, and a selection effect, since incidents tend to get reported more readily once congestion from them is already visible, which quietly links the incident feature to the very slowdown it is meant to help predict. This reporting delay is exactly why incidents help less than intuition suggests for a short-horizon prediction: by the time an incident is logged, the traffic model's own speed and flow features may already reflect the slowdown it caused, making the incident feature partially redundant rather than an early warning. Treating `created` as ground truth for when something happened without accounting for that lag is a common mistake, since it can make an incident look like it precedes a slowdown it actually follows.

The incident feed exposes several subtleties easy to get wrong: because reports are event-driven and irregularly spaced against the regular five-minute detector grid, joining incidents to that grid requires an explicit windowing decision, how far in space, how far in time counts as near, and the choice materially changes what an incident feature captures. Interval censoring on start and end times means the feed cannot cleanly answer whether there was an incident at exactly this station at exactly this minute, only whether one was reported nearby around this time, so any binary incident flag is a noisy proxy rather than ground truth. There is also a subtler leakage risk: `updated` can move forward in time as an incident's details are corrected, so using the latest known state of an incident record for a point-in-time feature, rather than what was known as of the prediction moment, leaks future information about the incident's own resolution.

At larger scale, incident-style event data is where the project touches an open research area: representing sparse, irregularly reported events, a marked point process, jointly with a dense, regular sensor grid, rather than crudely converting one into a flag on the other, is an active line of work in spatio-temporal modeling. The production question this raises is about latency versus completeness: a system that waits for 511's polled, human-reported incidents is always behind connected-vehicle or camera-based detection, so teams operating at scale increasingly fuse multiple asynchronous sources with different delay and coverage profiles, a harder sensor-fusion problem than joining one clean feed to one clean grid.

boolean-mask.def: A column of true/false, one per row, used to select rows: `df[df.speed < 35]`.
levels: A boolean mask is like putting a sticker on every row that says yes or no, and then you only keep the rows with a yes sticker.

A boolean mask is a column of True and False values, one for each row of a table, made by writing a comparison like `df.speed < 35`. Putting that mask inside square brackets, `df[df.speed < 35]`, keeps only the rows where the comparison was True. This is the main way to filter rows in pandas without writing a loop.

`df.speed < 35` compares every value in the `speed` column to 35 and returns a new column of booleans, the same length as `df`, one True or False per row. `df[mask]` then keeps only the rows where the mask is True, so `df[df.speed < 35]` returns every row where speed is below 35. Masks combine with `&` (and) and `|` (or), each side wrapped in parentheses: `df[(df.speed < 35) & (df.pct_obs > 50)]` keeps slow rows that are also well-observed.

A boolean mask works because pandas, and numpy underneath it, support elementwise comparison and indexing: the comparison produces an array of the same shape as the original, and indexing with that array is vectorized, evaluated in compiled C rather than a Python loop, which is why `df[mask]` is both idiomatic and fast on large tables. Masks compose with assignment too: `df.loc[mask, "speed"] = np.nan` sets a value only in the rows where the mask is True, which is exactly how this course's cleaning stage blanks impossible or low-confidence readings. A common failure mode is chained indexing, `df[mask]["speed"] = x`, which can silently write to a temporary copy instead of the original DataFrame; `df.loc[mask, "speed"] = x` avoids the ambiguity.

Boolean masking's elegance hides a real cost at scale: each mask allocates a new boolean array the size of the table, and chaining several conditions creates several intermediate arrays, which matters when a table has tens of millions of rows and memory, not compute, is the binding constraint, as it is on this project's 16 GB machine. NaN complicates masks in a way beginners miss: any comparison against NaN returns False, so `df.speed < 35` silently excludes already-missing rows rather than raising an error, which is usually the desired behavior but needs to be checked, not assumed. Practitioners sometimes reach for masks where `query()` or a database-style filter, in DuckDB or SQL, would be both faster and more memory-efficient at real scale, because those engines can push the filter down before materializing full columns rather than building an explicit mask array first.

At the scale where a single DataFrame no longer fits comfortably in memory, boolean masking's core idea, predicate-based row selection, survives but the implementation changes: columnar engines like DuckDB, Spark, or Arrow-backed pandas push predicates down into the storage layer, filtering during a scan rather than materializing a full mask over an already-loaded table. The recurring production lesson is that masking logic, which rows count as valid, out of range, or trustworthy, is itself part of the model and needs the same versioning and testing discipline as the model's weights, since a silently changed cleaning threshold can shift a metric as much as a real model change would.

chunking.def: Reading a file in pieces (`chunksize`) and keeping only what is needed from each, so memory stays small.
levels: If a book is too heavy to carry all at once, you read it one page at a time instead, and chunking is the computer doing the same trick with a giant file.

Chunking means reading a big file in smaller pieces instead of loading the whole thing into memory at once. In pandas, `pd.read_csv(path, chunksize=200_000)` returns an iterator that gives you two hundred thousand rows at a time, and you process each piece and keep only what you need before moving to the next. This matters for a file too large for the computer's memory, like a full day of PeMS data.

A day's PeMS file is around 200 MB compressed but expands to several gigabytes as a DataFrame, more than a 16 GB Mac can comfortably hold alongside everything else running. `for chunk in pd.read_csv(path, chunksize=200_000):` turns the read into a loop, where each `chunk` is its own small DataFrame; inside the loop you filter, clean, and keep only the rows you need, then discard the rest before the next chunk arrives. Streaming this way keeps peak memory bounded regardless of the file's total size, at the cost of processing rows in pieces rather than all at once.

Chunking trades memory for a constraint on the computation: any operation confined to one chunk, filtering, per-row transforms, simple aggregation, works cleanly, but operations that need to see the whole dataset at once, a global sort, a full groupby spanning chunk boundaries, need either a second pass or an accumulator carried across chunks. `chunksize` is the simplest form of this pattern; a Python generator using `yield` is the more general one, letting you write custom streaming logic, like line-by-line filtering of a gzipped file, rather than relying on pandas's built-in chunk iterator. Chunk size itself is a tuning knob: too small and per-chunk overhead dominates; too large and you are back to the original memory problem, so 200,000 rows here is chosen empirically for this project's row width and the machine's memory budget.

The general principle behind chunking is that of any streaming data pipeline: idempotence, rerunning gives the same result, bounded memory independent of input size, and careful handling of state that must persist across chunks, like a running mean, which otherwise silently reintroduces the memory-growth problem chunking was meant to solve. A subtlety practitioners often miss: chunk boundaries are arbitrary with respect to the data's own structure, so a computation needing all of one entity's rows together, all of one station's day, for example, can be split across two chunks unless the file is pre-sorted or chunks are read to respect entity boundaries, which is why some pipelines chunk by group rather than by fixed row count. Columnar formats like Parquet make a different, often better, tradeoff available: predicate and column pushdown reads only the needed columns and row groups directly from disk, avoiding chunking's per-chunk Python overhead entirely for many workloads.

At production scale, chunking generalizes into stream processing proper: systems like Spark or Flink face the same core tension between memory, latency, and correctness under out-of-order or late-arriving data, and the chunking pattern here, bounded memory, one pass, keep only what is needed, is the same idea a distributed stream processor implements with watermarks and windowing instead of a fixed `chunksize`. The open engineering question at scale is less about reading a single file in pieces and more about maintaining correctness, exactly-once processing, consistent state across restarts, when the file is actually an unbounded, continuously arriving stream, a substantially harder problem than the batch chunking used to clean one PeMS day.

unit.def: The thing a row describes: one station at one timestamp.
levels: The unit is just what one little card in your card pile is about; here, each card is about one road-watcher at one moment in time.

The unit of a prediction problem is what one row of data represents. In this project, the unit is one station at one five-minute timestamp: every row is this detector, at this moment. Getting the unit clear first is what lets you decide what the inputs and the target should be.

A prediction problem has four parts, and the unit is the first: what one row describes, here station and timestamp, meaning one detector's reading at one five-minute mark. The other three parts build on it: the inputs are everything known about that unit at or before its timestamp, the target is a yes-or-no fact about its future, and the metric scores how good the guesses were. Written formally, the unit indexes a panel: feature vector x_{s,t} and target y_{s,t} both belong to the pair of station s and time t.

Fixing the unit as station and time is a modeling decision, not a fact about the world, and it determines what one training example means: every row in the training table is one station's state at one moment, and the model learns a function from that unit's inputs to that unit's target, treating different station-time pairs as separate examples even though nearby ones are strongly correlated. This choice has direct consequences for evaluation: because units at the same station and nearby times are not independent, a random train and validation split across units leaks information in a way a naive reading of more training rows is always better would miss, which is why this course splits by time instead. Choosing a coarser or finer unit changes the whole problem: a unit of freeway segment and hour would need different features and give a different, smoother prediction task than station and five-minute mark does.

The unit interacts with almost every other modeling choice in ways that are easy to get backwards: it sets the granularity of leakage checks, you must ask was this known for this exact unit at this exact time, not just was this known, the granularity of the metric, average precision computed per unit pools together very different traffic regimes unless slicing by station or time of day is done separately, and the granularity of the model's own assumptions, logistic regression per row assumes units are conditionally independent given their features, an assumption graph and sequence models exist specifically to relax. Practitioners sometimes redefine the unit implicitly and inconsistently across a pipeline, for instance aggregating to station and hour for one feature but leaving the target at station and five minutes, which silently misaligns training rows without raising an error.

At larger scale, the choice of unit is often the single design decision with the biggest downstream effect on what a system can and cannot do: a unit too coarse cannot express a fast-moving three-minute stall, a unit too fine multiplies the number of predictions a serving system must produce and calibrate, so production spatio-temporal systems often support multiple resolutions and reconcile them, rather than committing to one fixed unit the way this course does for pedagogical clarity. An open research question is how to let the unit itself be learned or adapted, dynamically choosing coarser units where traffic is stable and finer ones where it is volatile, rather than fixing station and five minutes uniformly across a whole freeway network.

feature-engineering.def: Deciding and computing the input columns: lags, rolling statistics, time-of-day circle, holidays, neighbor readings.
levels: Feature engineering is picking which clues to write down before you guess, like noticing the sky is grey and the wind picked up before guessing it will rain.

Feature engineering means deciding which input columns to compute from the raw data and then actually computing them. For the traffic project this includes lag features, the speed 5 or 15 minutes ago, rolling statistics, the average speed over the last half hour, and neighbor readings, what the upstream and downstream stations are seeing right now. Good features often matter more than which algorithm you use afterward.

A feature is one input column, and feature engineering is the process of turning raw signals into a table the model can use, following one strict rule: every feature must be computable only from rows at or before the current timestamp. `g = df.groupby("station_id")` groups the data so features stay inside one station, and from there `g.speed.shift(3)` makes a lag feature, speed 15 minutes ago, while `g.speed.rolling(6).mean()` makes a rolling average over the last half hour. Time of day is usually encoded as a circle, sine and cosine of the time, rather than a raw hour number, so that 23:59 and 00:01 read as close together instead of far apart.

Feature engineering is best thought of as hypothesis-making: each feature encodes a specific belief about what predicts the target, momentum, spatial propagation, or periodicity, and a feature's usefulness is really a test of that hypothesis once the model is trained. The one invariant across every feature in this course is the leakage rule, computed only from information available at or before the prediction timestamp, because a single feature that peeks even five minutes into the future can make an offline metric look excellent while the same feature is undefined or wrong at serving time. Correlation with the target is a cheap first check, `speed_lag_0` correlates less with `y_60` than with `y_15`, for example, because momentum decays with horizon, but it does not replace fitting a model, since features can matter jointly, or after interacting with each other, in ways a single correlation coefficient cannot show.

The subtlety practitioners get wrong most often is not computing a leaky feature outright but computing a feature correctly in training and differently at serving time, point-in-time correctness, since a rolling mean computed once over a whole historical table and a rolling mean computed incrementally as new rows arrive in production can differ subtly at the edges, especially around missing data or station gaps. Feature engineering also interacts with model choice in ways easy to underweight: gradient-boosted trees can find some nonlinear interactions and thresholds on their own, reducing the need for hand-crafted interaction features that a linear model like logistic regression requires explicitly. A well-designed feature set is also a form of documentation: a feature importance ranking that surprises a domain expert is often a sign of leakage or a data bug, not a genuine discovery, so surprising importances deserve suspicion before celebration.

At production scale, feature engineering becomes a systems problem as much as a modeling one: the same feature logic must run identically in a batch training pipeline and a low-latency serving path, exactly the point-in-time correctness problem that feature stores with time-travel joins exist to solve, and this course's small-scale answer, one shared feature module used by both paths plus a golden-file test comparing them bit for bit, is a miniature of that same discipline. The open research direction is reducing how much of this work is manual at all: learned feature representations increasingly substitute for hand-built lags and rolling statistics, though in practice teams still keep interpretable hand-engineered features alongside learned ones, because the hand-built features are what a human can audit when a prediction goes wrong.

threshold.def: The score above which an alert fires. Chosen on validation to meet a required precision.
levels: A threshold is a line in the sand: if your worry-o-meter goes above it, you ring the bell; if it stays below, you stay quiet.

A threshold, written τ (tau), is the score above which the model's alert fires. The model outputs a number between 0 and 1 for each row, and if that number is above τ, the system says slow traffic is coming; otherwise it stays silent. The threshold is chosen after training, on a separate validation set, not decided in advance.

A model gives each row a probability-like score, for example `p_30`, between 0 and 1, and an alert fires when that score exceeds τ. Choosing τ is a business decision translated into a precision requirement, for instance at least half of all alarms must be correct, and `precision_recall_curve` gives the tool: it returns precision and recall at every possible threshold, so you scan for the lowest threshold meeting the precision bar, `thr[ok[0]]`, since scikit-learn orders thresholds increasing and the lowest one meeting the bar keeps the most recall. Save τ per horizon into `models/calibration.json` so it can be re-tuned later without retraining the underlying model.

The threshold is deliberately kept separate from model training because it encodes a cost tradeoff, false alarms versus missed jams, that belongs to the product, not to the loss function the model was fit with: logistic regression and LightGBM here are both trained to produce a well-ranked score, and only afterward is a single operating point chosen on that score. This separation lets the required precision change, say from 50% to 70%, by re-running only the threshold search on the validation split, not retraining, since the underlying ranking is unaffected. It also means threshold choice is only as good as the calibration of the underlying scores; if the model's probabilities are systematically too high or too low, a fixed precision target picked on validation may not transfer to a differently-distributed period, like a holiday week, without recalibration.

A subtlety many practitioners miss is that a threshold picked once on a single validation window is a point estimate with sampling variance, and it can shift meaningfully if re-derived on a different slice of time, since traffic is non-stationary; bootstrap resampling across validation days, as this course does, gives a distribution of plausible thresholds, not just one number, and reporting that range is more honest than reporting τ to three decimal places. There is also a subtle asymmetry in the optimal-decision derivation: writing expected cost as a function of the decision shows that alerting is worth it exactly when the predicted probability exceeds the false-alarm cost divided by the sum of false-alarm and miss costs, which means the right precision target is not a fixed universal number but depends on how costly a missed jam is relative to a false alert, a business input the threshold search can only reflect, not derive.

In production, a single global threshold rarely survives contact with a large, heterogeneous deployment: different stations, times of day, or user segments can have different cost structures or different score distributions, so systems at scale often move to per-segment or continuously recalibrated thresholds, sometimes chosen automatically to hold precision constant as the underlying score distribution drifts, a harder and more fragile problem than the one-time offline threshold search this course teaches. An open production question is how to detect threshold staleness, a τ that once met its precision target but silently no longer does because the world changed, before it shows up as a spike in complaints about false or missed alerts.

parameters.def: Parameters are learned from data; hyperparameters (learning rate, number of leaves) are chosen before training.
levels: Parameters are the numbers a robot slowly figures out by practicing, like how hard to push a swing; hyperparameters are the rules you set for the robot's practice before it even starts, like how many times it gets to try.

Parameters, also called weights, are the numbers a model learns from the training data, adjusted a little bit at a time to make its guesses better. Hyperparameters, like the learning rate or the number of leaves in a tree, are settings you choose before training even begins, and they are not learned. In logistic regression, `w` and `b` are the parameters; how big a step gradient descent takes each round is a hyperparameter.

A parameter is a number the training algorithm updates, like the weight vector `w` and bias `b` in logistic regression, which start random or zero and are nudged every epoch by `w -= eta * gw`. A hyperparameter is chosen up front and held fixed during that training run, for example `learning_rate=0.05` and `num_leaves=63` in LightGBM, or `eta` in the hand-written gradient descent loop. You cannot fit hyperparameters the same way you fit parameters; instead you try several values and keep whichever gives the best validation score.

Parameters live inside the model's functional form and are optimized by minimizing a loss function on training data, gradient descent for logistic regression, leaf-splitting for LightGBM, so the number of parameters is fixed by the model's architecture, one weight per feature plus a bias for logistic regression, and their values are entirely determined by the data and the optimizer. Hyperparameters, by contrast, control the model's capacity and the optimization process itself, and they cannot be chosen by minimizing training loss, since more capacity, deeper trees, smaller `min_data_in_leaf`, always fits training data at least as well and often overfits; hyperparameters are instead selected using a held-out validation score. This distinction generalizes past logistic regression and trees: in a neural network the weight matrices are parameters, while the number of layers, hidden width, and learning rate are hyperparameters, and the same overfitting risk applies to searching over hyperparameters as to fitting parameters.

A subtlety many practitioners skip is that hyperparameter search is itself a form of fitting, and choosing among many configurations on a single validation split is optimistic in exactly the way choosing parameters on the training split is; nested or rolling-origin validation, where an outer split evaluates the whole selection process, is the honest but more expensive answer, and skipping it quietly inflates a reported metric. Another common confusion is treating more hyperparameters tuned as strictly better: heavy hyperparameter search on a small or noisy validation set can overfit to that split's particular noise, which is why this course emphasizes checking whether reported gains hold up across rolling folds, not just one split. There is also a real cost asymmetry: gradient-based parameters update cheaply via backpropagation on millions of examples at once, while most hyperparameter search methods treat each configuration as an expensive black-box evaluation requiring a full retrain, which is why hyperparameter tuning is often the more compute-expensive half of a modeling project despite touching far fewer numbers.

At the scale of large neural networks, the parameter and hyperparameter line has started to blur: scaling laws let researchers predict good hyperparameters, learning rate, batch size, for a large model from experiments on much smaller ones, effectively treating hyperparameter choice itself as something learnable across scale rather than something re-searched from scratch for every model size. Hyperparameter importance analysis, understanding which dials actually matter for a given architecture and dataset, is itself now a research tool, and the reproducibility concern this raises is real: many reported gains in the literature turn out to be within the noise of the tuning budget used, meaning the tuning process, not just the parameters found, deserves to be reported and scrutinized.

gradient-check.def: Comparing the formula's gradient with a brute-force slope from nudging one parameter. Done once per new model.
levels: A gradient check is like double-checking your math homework by trying a slightly different number and seeing if the answer moves the way you expected.

A gradient check compares the gradient formula you derived on paper with a brute-force estimate: nudge one weight up a tiny bit, measure how the loss changes, nudge it down the same tiny bit, measure again, and see if the difference matches your formula. It catches sign errors and other bugs in a hand-derived gradient before you trust it to train a model. You do this once when you write new gradient math, not every time you train.

The numerical gradient check nudges one parameter by a small `eps`, say 1e-5, computes the loss before and after, and estimates the slope as the loss at w plus eps minus the loss at w minus eps, divided by 2·eps, the same idea as a derivative from calculus. This numerical estimate is compared against the formula's gradient at that same parameter, and the two should agree to a couple of decimal places once rounded with `np.round(x, 3)`. If they do not agree, the usual cause is a genuine bug in the formula, though too few training epochs or too large a learning rate can also make gradients look inconsistent for unrelated reasons.

A gradient derived by hand can be wrong by a sign, a missing factor, or a transposed matrix and still let training run, only badly or slowly, which is what makes gradient checking essential rather than optional: bad gradients degrade performance in ways easy to misattribute to the model, the data, or the learning rate instead of to the bug that is actually there. The check works because the two-sided finite-difference estimate has error of order eps², much more accurate than a one-sided estimate, so with a well-chosen eps, small enough to be accurate, large enough to avoid floating-point cancellation, the numerical and analytic gradients should match to several significant figures for a correct implementation. Gradient checks are run on a handful of parameters and rows, not the full model, since finite differences require one full forward pass per parameter checked and would be prohibitively slow at full scale.

In practice the check is run once, right after deriving new gradient math by hand, and then relied upon: once verified, the analytic gradient is what trains the model going forward, so the check functions like a unit test for calculus rather than a runtime safeguard. A common mistake is checking gradients on a model in an unusual numerical regime, all-zero weights, or with a learning rate or loss scale that masks a real bug, which is why the check is typically done at random, nonzero initial weights. When automatic differentiation frameworks like PyTorch are used instead of hand-derived formulas, gradient checking mostly disappears for standard operations, since the framework's own autograd is tested far more thoroughly than any individual researcher's from-scratch derivation, but it reappears for custom, non-standard operations where autograd cannot be trusted blindly either.

At scale, exhaustive finite-difference checking of every parameter in a billion-parameter model is computationally infeasible, so production and research teams instead check gradients on small unit-test-sized components in isolation, a single custom layer, a new loss function, before it is composed into a much larger model where a bug would be far harder to localize. The broader lesson gradient checking teaches generalizes past this one technique: verifying a complex numerical system against a slower, simpler, independently-derived version of the same computation is a general debugging strategy, and teams that skip this step for new model components are disproportionately represented among the debugging sessions that eat days instead of hours.

feature-importance.def: Importance by gain totals how much each feature reduced the loss; SHAP splits one prediction into per-feature contributions.
levels: Feature importance is like asking which clue helped the most after guessing whether it will rain, and finding out that dark clouds helped a lot more than it being Tuesday.

Feature importance ranks which input columns mattered most to a trained model's predictions. One common kind, importance by gain, adds up how much each feature reduced the model's error across every split that used it in a tree-based model like LightGBM. SHAP goes further and explains one single prediction, showing how much each feature pushed that particular row's score up or down.

Importance by gain sums, across every tree and every split point in a gradient-boosted model, how much loss that split reduced, then attributes that reduction to whichever feature was split on, giving one importance score per feature averaged across the whole model. SHAP, SHapley Additive exPlanations, instead explains individual predictions: `shap.TreeExplainer(m)` builds an explainer, and `shap_values` computes, for a sample of rows, exactly how much each feature contributed, positive or negative, to that row's specific prediction. A `summary_plot` then shows the distribution of these per-row contributions across features, a richer picture than one global gain number per feature.

The two measures answer different questions and can disagree: gain-based importance is biased toward high-cardinality features that offer the tree many possible split points, and toward features used near the root of many trees, regardless of whether those splits generalize, while TreeSHAP gives exact, theoretically grounded per-row attributions based on Shapley values from cooperative game theory, at the cost of being much more expensive to compute, which is why this course samples twenty thousand rows rather than running it on the full validation set. Neither measure establishes causation: a feature can rank highly because it is genuinely causal, or because it is a strong proxy for something else that is, and a tree model cannot distinguish the two from correlational training data alone. Feature importance is best used as a debugging and hypothesis-generation tool; if a feature that should not matter, an ID column, a data artifact, ranks highly, that is usually a sign of a leak or bug, not a real signal.

A subtlety practitioners get wrong constantly is treating high importance as proof a feature is useful and low importance as proof it is not: correlated features split importance between them, so removing a low-importance feature that is actually highly correlated with a high-importance one can change little, while removing one of two correlated important features can dramatically shift the other's apparent importance without changing the model's overall performance. SHAP's additivity, per-row contributions sum to the model's output minus its baseline, is a real theoretical guarantee, but interaction effects, where two features matter jointly in a way neither does alone, get distributed across both features' individual SHAP values in ways that can undersell how much the interaction itself matters. The common misreading, that feature importance shows causation, deserves explicit pushback: it shows what the trees used to reduce loss, and a proxy for the true cause ranks exactly as high as the cause itself.

At production scale, feature importance and SHAP serve less as a way to explain any single prediction to an end user, which raises its own fairness and interpretability concerns when done naively, and more as a monitoring tool: tracking how feature importances drift over time flags when the world has changed underneath a deployed model, for instance a feature that used to matter losing importance as its relationship to the target shifts. Computing SHAP values at serving scale for every prediction is often too expensive, so production systems typically compute it offline on samples for monitoring rather than online for every request, and an open engineering problem is making faithful, cheap real-time explanations available where regulation or product needs actually require per-prediction accountability.

adjacency-matrix.def: An N × N table of 0/1 saying which stations are neighbors. `A @ h` sums each station's neighbors' vectors.
levels: An adjacency matrix is a big chart where every road-watcher gets a row and a column, and you put a 1 wherever two watchers are next-door neighbors, and a 0 everywhere else.

An adjacency matrix is a grid with one row and one column for every station, N rows by N columns for N stations. Entry (i, j) is 1 if station j is station i's neighbor and 0 otherwise. If each station also has a summary vector `h` of its recent traffic, then `A @ h` adds up each station's neighbors' vectors, one sum per station.

For N stations, the adjacency matrix A is N × N, with A[i, j] = 1 exactly when station j is a neighbor of station i, and 0 otherwise. If `h` is a matrix with one row per station holding that station's hidden summary vector, `A @ h` computes, for every station at once, the sum of its neighbors' vectors, a single matrix multiplication doing what would otherwise be a loop over every station and its neighbors. On a directed road, upstream and downstream are different relationships, so this course actually uses two matrices, `A_up` and `A_down`, rather than one symmetric one.

The adjacency matrix is what turns a road network into something linear algebra can operate on: multiplying by A is a form of message passing, where each station's next representation incorporates a sum of its neighbors' current representations, and stacking this operation K times lets information propagate K hops across the graph. For a directed graph like a freeway, A is not symmetric, and using separate `A_up` and `A_down` matrices, as this course does, lets a station's representation update differently depending on whether information is flowing with or against the direction of traffic, which matters because a slowdown that starts downstream propagates upstream, not the other way around. Dense adjacency matrices are wasteful for sparse, realistic road graphs, where most station pairs are not neighbors, so real implementations typically store A as a sparse matrix or an edge list once N is large.

A subtlety that trips up newcomers to graph neural networks is that raw adjacency, unnormalized 0/1 entries, can make message-passing outputs grow with a station's number of neighbors, so most practical formulations normalize A, for instance dividing each row by its degree, or using a symmetric normalization involving the degree matrix, which is closer to a true averaging operation and keeps values from exploding as layers stack. The adjacency matrix also encodes a modeling assumption about what neighbor means, geographic adjacency, direct road connectivity, or a learned, adaptive adjacency, as in Graph WaveNet, that the model fits from data rather than assumes from geometry, and this choice matters enormously: a fixed geographic adjacency cannot represent that a distant on-ramp sometimes affects a station more than its immediate physical neighbor during unusual traffic patterns. Any graph representation must also respect permutation invariance, the result should not depend on the arbitrary order stations happen to be listed in, which rules out simply treating the adjacency matrix as an image.

At the scale of a full metro or state-wide road network, a full N × N dense adjacency matrix stops being practical, both because most of it is zero and because the memory to store and multiply by it grows quadratically, so production systems store sparse adjacency and use sparse matrix multiplication or explicit neighbor-sampling schemes rather than dense `A @ h`. An open research direction is learning the adjacency itself rather than fixing it from road geometry, since the true functional relationship between stations does not always match physical adjacency, and letting a model learn or adapt this structure from data can outperform a fixed geographic graph, at the cost of losing the physical interpretability a hand-built adjacency matrix provides.

resident-memory.def: The RAM a process is actually using, logged per stage so a 16 GB machine never swaps.
levels: Resident memory is how much of the computer's thinking-space a program is actually using right now, like how much room your toys actually take up on the floor versus how much floor there is.

Resident memory, or RSS (resident set size), is the amount of RAM a running program is actually using at a given moment, measured in bytes and usually reported in gigabytes. In this project, every pipeline stage prints its own RSS at the end, using Python's `psutil` library, so you can see which stage uses the most memory. This matters because a 16 GB Mac mini will slow to a crawl, swapping, if any one stage grows too large.

`psutil.Process(os.getpid())` gets a handle on the currently running program, and `.memory_info().rss` returns its resident set size in bytes, the memory currently held in RAM rather than paged out or never allocated; dividing by 1e9 converts that to gigabytes. This course has every stage print one structured line at the end, like a name, an input, a runtime, and a peak memory figure, easy to search across a log. Watching RSS across stages catches a stage quietly growing toward the machine's 16 GB limit before it starts swapping and slowing everything down.

RSS differs from a process's virtual memory size, which can be much larger, including memory reserved but not yet touched, and from its total allocated memory, which can include pages later reclaimed by the operating system, which is why RSS specifically, memory actually resident in physical RAM, is the number that predicts whether a machine will start swapping. Logging RSS per stage rather than only at the end of a whole pipeline is deliberate: a spike that happens and is released mid-stage would be invisible in a single end-to-end peak measurement but is exactly the kind of transient spike that can push a shared machine into swap. On a laptop or a single Mac mini, where there is no cluster to spread load across, RSS becomes the primary resource constraint that decides whether streaming is optional or mandatory for a given stage.

A subtlety about RSS specific to a Unix-like OS: shared library pages, numpy's compiled C code, for instance, are counted in every process's RSS that maps them, so RSS is not perfectly additive across processes, which matters when estimating whether several stages could safely run concurrently rather than sequentially. Python's own memory behavior adds further wrinkles: the interpreter often does not return freed memory to the operating system immediately, so RSS can stay elevated after a large DataFrame is deleted, giving a falsely alarming impression that memory is leaking when it is really just not yet reclaimed by the allocator. Peak RSS during a computation, not the RSS at the moment you happen to check, is what actually causes swapping, so logging only at a stage's end can still miss a transient in-stage peak that briefly exceeded available memory.

At the scale of a fleet of machines or a shared cluster, per-process RSS logging generalizes into full resource monitoring and cgroup-based memory limits, where a process exceeding its allotted RSS gets killed by the scheduler rather than allowed to swap and degrade the whole machine, a much harsher but more predictable failure mode than the silent slowdown a single unmonitored Mac mini experiences. The production discipline this project's simple per-stage RSS logging is a miniature of is capacity planning: knowing each stage's memory footprint precisely enough to pack jobs onto shared hardware without over- or under-provisioning, which for on-device or edge deployment also has to account for other processes competing for the same fixed memory.

bernoulli.def: Bernoulli models a single yes/no outcome with one probability p; Poisson models a count of events, like cars passing, with one rate parameter λ.
levels: A Bernoulli is like flipping one coin: it lands on one of two things, heads or tails, yes or no. A Poisson is like counting how many cars zoom by your window in a minute; some minutes have more, some have fewer, but there is a usual number they cluster around.

A Bernoulli distribution describes one yes-or-no outcome, like whether a station is in a slow episode, with a single number p for how likely yes is. A Poisson distribution describes a count of things that happen in a fixed span, like how many cars pass a station in five minutes, with a single number λ, the average count, that also sets how spread out the counts are. Both are simple building blocks: Bernoulli for single yes/no events, Poisson for counts of events.

A Bernoulli random variable takes value 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1 − p; the slow-or-not label used throughout this course is Bernoulli, and logistic regression is trained to estimate p for each row. A Poisson random variable counts events in a fixed interval and takes any non-negative integer value 0, 1, 2, …, with probability λᵏe^(−λ)/k!, where λ is both the mean and the variance; PeMS's `flow` column, cars counted per five minutes, is naturally modeled this way. A Poisson generalized linear model, predicting λ from features rather than assuming it constant, is one way to model flow directly instead of treating it as an ordinary continuous number.

The Bernoulli distribution is the foundation of binary classification: logistic regression is exactly maximum-likelihood estimation for a Bernoulli outcome whose success probability p is a sigmoid of a linear score, and minimizing cross-entropy loss is mathematically identical to maximizing that Bernoulli likelihood. The Poisson distribution assumes its mean equals its variance, a strong assumption that real count data, including traffic flow, often violates through overdispersion, variance exceeding the mean, from unmodeled heterogeneity between stations or bursty events, which is why a Negative Binomial or a Gamma-distributed generalized linear model is often preferred over plain Poisson for messy count data. Both distributions belong to the exponential family, which is why they slot cleanly into the generalized linear model framework: a linear predictor, a link function, and a distribution matched to the outcome type.

A subtlety with the Bernoulli and logistic setup that practitioners often miss is that the maximum-likelihood estimate does not exist, coefficients diverge to infinity, under quasi-complete separation, where some feature or combination of features perfectly predicts the outcome in the training data, which regularization, an L2 penalty equivalent to a Gaussian prior producing the MAP estimate, fixes in practice even when it is not diagnosed explicitly as a separation problem. With Poisson models, the equal mean-variance assumption is violated so routinely in real count data that fitting plain Poisson and reporting its standard errors without checking for overdispersion is a common and consequential mistake, since standard errors come out too small, understating real uncertainty, when the variance is actually larger than the mean assumes. Both distributions also connect to a broader idea worth knowing: the canonical link function for each, logit for Bernoulli, log for Poisson, is what makes the score-residual gradient form clean and iteratively reweighted least squares converge quickly, a property that is elegant for these two distributions specifically and not guaranteed for an arbitrary distribution-link pairing.

At production scale, Bernoulli and Poisson assumptions rarely survive intact: real binary labels have measurement noise and label ambiguity that a plain Bernoulli likelihood does not model, and real event counts are typically overdispersed, zero-inflated, or dependent across time in ways that motivate hierarchical or mixture extensions, a Beta-Binomial for a station's varying slow-rate, a zero-inflated Poisson for mostly-empty count data, rather than the textbook single-parameter versions. These distributions remain foundational anyway because they are the simplest, most tractable building blocks that everything more complex, generalized linear mixed models, Bayesian hierarchical models, deep learning heads with a Poisson or Bernoulli output layer, is built from and compared against, so understanding exactly where their assumptions break is what tells a practitioner when a fancier model is actually needed rather than merely fashionable.

laplace.def: Laplace's method approximates a hard-to-integrate probability distribution with a Gaussian centered at its peak; a related Laplace distribution generates noise for privacy.
levels: Imagine a lumpy hill and you want to describe its shape quickly, so you just draw a smooth round bump at the very top instead of tracing every bump exactly. That quick round-bump guess is the idea behind Laplace's method.

Laplace's method is a shortcut for describing a complicated probability distribution: instead of working out its exact, possibly lumpy shape, you approximate it with a simple bell curve centered at its highest point. This makes hard math problems, like combining many uncertain guesses in a Bayesian model, solvable quickly, at the cost of losing some accuracy away from the peak. A related idea with the same name, Laplace noise, is a specific kind of random static added to a number to keep it private.

Given a probability distribution that is hard to work with directly, Laplace's method finds its peak, the mode, measures how sharply the distribution curves there, using the second derivative, and fits a Gaussian with that same peak and curvature as an approximation. This is used in this course for Bayesian logistic regression, where the true posterior over the weights has no clean formula but a Gaussian approximation around its most likely weights does. Separately, the Laplace distribution, a specific bell-shaped-but-pointier curve, also called double-exponential, is used to generate noise for differential privacy: adding Laplace-distributed noise to a released statistic like an hourly average speed hides any one individual's contribution.

Laplace's method works by taking a second-order Taylor expansion of the log of the target distribution around its mode, which cancels the linear term, since the derivative is zero at the mode, and leaves a quadratic term whose coefficient is exactly the curvature there; exponentiating that quadratic approximation gives a Gaussian, so the approximation is only as good as the true distribution's actual shape near the mode. It is exact when the true distribution is already Gaussian and degrades as the true distribution becomes more skewed, multimodal, or heavy-tailed, since a single Gaussian at one peak cannot represent multiple modes or asymmetric tails. The unrelated-but-same-name Laplace distribution used for differential privacy has density proportional to e^(−|x|/b), heavier-tailed than a Gaussian, and its scale b is set as a function of the desired privacy budget ε and the query's sensitivity, the largest amount one person's data could change the released statistic.

A subtlety practitioners often gloss over with Laplace's approximation is that it captures local curvature at the mode but nothing about the distribution's global shape, so for a posterior with a mode near a boundary, like a probability near 0 or 1, or with multiple comparably likely modes, the Gaussian approximation can be badly miscalibrated even though it is exact to second order at the point it was built from; more expensive alternatives, MCMC, variational inference, are the honest fix when this matters. Model comparison via the marginal likelihood is one place Laplace's method earns its keep beyond convenience: it gives an automatic complexity penalty without ad hoc regularization terms, because a model whose posterior is sharply peaked gets a different evidence score than one whose posterior stays broad. On the privacy side, the tradeoff practitioners get wrong is treating ε as a free knob to tune for good utility rather than as the actual privacy guarantee it is; a large ε makes the released statistic more useful and less private, and choosing it after seeing how noisy small ε makes the results defeats its purpose.

At production scale, Laplace's approximation is increasingly the fast, cheap option compared to full MCMC or variational inference for calibrating uncertainty in a deployed model, and last-layer Laplace, applying the approximation only to a neural network's final layer, is a specific technique used to get calibrated uncertainty out of an otherwise deterministic deep network without retraining it as fully Bayesian. On the privacy side, Laplace-mechanism differential privacy is one tool among several, the Gaussian mechanism, more recent DP-SGD-style training-time noise, used in production systems that release aggregate statistics, and the open engineering question is less the mechanism itself and more the accounting: composing many DP-protected queries over a system's lifetime while tracking a total privacy budget without it silently exceeding what was promised.

sigmoid-2.def: The S-shaped function σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(−z)) that squashes any number into a probability between 0 and 1.
levels: The sigmoid is a magic squisher: you feed it any number, huge or tiny, and it always hands back a number between 0 and 1, like squeezing a big sponge down to fit in your pocket.

The sigmoid function takes any number, positive or negative, and squashes it into a range between 0 and 1, shaped like a stretched-out S when you draw it. A big positive number in gives a result close to 1, a big negative number gives a result close to 0, and 0 gives exactly 0.5. This makes it perfect for turning a raw score into something that reads as a probability.

The formula is σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)), and in code, `def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))`, applied to a whole array of scores at once. Logistic regression computes a score z = w·x + b for each row, then passes it through σ to get a probability p between 0 and 1; z = 0 gives p = 0.5, the no-information point. The sigmoid's own derivative has a clean form, σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), which is what makes logistic regression's gradient simple to derive.

The sigmoid is the inverse of the logit, or log-odds, function log(p/(1−p)), so it exactly translates an unbounded linear score into a valid probability, which is the mathematical justification for using it as logistic regression's output nonlinearity rather than an arbitrary choice. Its derivative, σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)), is what makes the gradient of cross-entropy loss with respect to the model's raw score reduce to simply p − y, the prediction error, since the sigmoid's derivative cancels neatly against the log-loss's own derivative through the chain rule. In deep networks, the sigmoid saturates for large |z|, its derivative approaches 0 at both extremes, so a very confident, very wrong prediction produces a tiny gradient and learns extremely slowly, which is one reason ReLU, not the sigmoid, is the default activation inside modern hidden layers even though sigmoid remains standard as a final binary output layer.

The saturation problem is more consequential than it first appears: stacking many sigmoid layers compounds vanishing gradients multiplicatively through the chain rule, historically a central obstacle to training deep networks before ReLU and better initialization schemes became standard, so the sigmoid's near-universal 1990s role as a hidden-layer activation has been almost entirely replaced, while its role as a final binary-output squashing function remains unchanged and appropriate. A numerical subtlety practitioners hit in practice: computing the sigmoid directly for very negative z can overflow, so a numerically stable implementation branches on the sign of z or, more commonly, frameworks avoid computing the sigmoid explicitly at all and instead combine it with cross-entropy into a single numerically stable operation, `BCEWithLogitsLoss` in PyTorch, which never computes intermediate probabilities near exactly 0 or 1. The clip used in this course, `np.clip(sigmoid(...), 1e-7, 1 - 1e-7)`, exists for the same reason: log(0) is undefined, and an unclipped, perfectly confident but wrong prediction produces an infinite loss and gradient.

At production scale, the sigmoid's role has narrowed but not disappeared: it remains the standard way to turn a final logit into a probability for binary classification and multi-label problems, and fused implementations like BCEWithLogitsLoss are the default because they are both faster and more numerically stable than computing the sigmoid and the log-loss separately. Research interest in sigmoid-like functions has shifted from activation function for hidden layers, a largely settled question in favor of ReLU-family functions, to newer uses like smooth gating mechanisms, the sigmoid gates inside an LSTM or GRU, or Swish and SiLU-style activations that multiply a linear unit by a sigmoid of itself, where its bounded, differentiable, monotonic shape is exploited deliberately rather than merely inherited from older architectures.

svm.def: A classifier that finds the widest possible margin between classes, using kernels to draw curved boundaries; strong on small data, slow on millions of rows.
levels: Imagine drawing a line between red and blue marbles so that the fattest possible gap separates them. An SVM is a computer that finds exactly that widest gap.

A support vector machine, or SVM, is a classifier that draws a boundary between two groups of points, choosing the boundary that leaves the biggest possible margin, or gap, on either side. Only the points closest to the boundary, called support vectors, actually determine where the line goes. SVMs can also use kernels to draw curved boundaries instead of straight lines, when a straight line cannot separate the groups well.

An SVM finds the line, or with more features a hyperplane, that maximizes the margin, the distance to the nearest point of either class, rather than just any line that separates them, which tends to generalize better than the first separating line found. The soft margin version allows some points to sit inside the margin or even on the wrong side, controlled by a penalty parameter, so the SVM works even when the classes are not perfectly separable. A kernel, like the RBF kernel, lets the SVM effectively draw curved decision boundaries by measuring similarity in a higher-dimensional space without ever computing that space directly.

The SVM is formulated as a convex optimization problem, maximize the margin subject to correctly classifying, or softly penalizing errors on, every training point, and its dual formulation reveals that the resulting decision boundary depends only on the support vectors, with every other training point's coefficient equal to zero at the optimum. The kernel trick exploits the fact that the dual problem only needs inner products between data points, not the points themselves, so replacing the ordinary dot product with a kernel function implicitly computes an inner product in a much higher-dimensional feature space, letting the SVM separate classes that are not linearly separable in the original space, without ever constructing that space explicitly. SVMs use hinge loss rather than logistic regression's cross-entropy, which produces a maximum-margin rather than a maximum-likelihood boundary, and they need feature scaling to work well, since the margin's geometry is distorted by features on very different numeric scales.

The Bayes-optimal-classification view situates the SVM among its competitors: it is a large-margin discriminative model, unlike naive Bayes, a generative model with a factorized likelihood assumption, or k-nearest neighbors, which estimates the posterior locally and is consistent as k grows with n but suffers the curse of dimensionality; the SVM's margin-based generalization theory connects it to boosting's own margin arguments in a way that is theoretically elegant but does not fully explain either method's practical success. The dominant practical limitation practitioners run into is scale: standard SVM training is roughly quadratic to cubic in the number of training examples because the dual optimization involves an n×n kernel matrix, which makes SVMs strong on small, clean datasets, a few thousand to tens of thousands of rows, but impractical on the millions of rows a project like this one's traffic data has, where gradient-boosted trees train comparably well in a fraction of the time.
