Kernel choice and its hyperparameters, like the RBF kernel's bandwidth, matter enormously and are not learned from data the way SVM's own weights are, requiring the same held-out-validation hyperparameter search as any other model family.

SVMs remain genuinely useful in small-sample scientific settings, bioinformatics, some scientific measurement tasks, where data is expensive and clean and the classical margin-maximization theory's generalization guarantees are worth the computational cost, but they have been largely superseded by gradient-boosted trees and deep networks for the large, messy, tabular or unstructured datasets that dominate industrial machine learning, including this project's traffic data. Their lasting contribution is conceptual rather than a still-dominant production tool: the kernel trick they popularized underlies Gaussian processes and other kernel methods still actively used for small-data, uncertainty-aware modeling, and margin theory remains a live research thread connecting classical statistical learning theory to why certain deep learning training procedures generalize as well as they empirically do.

convolution.def: Sliding a small filter across data to compute a local weighted sum at every position, reused for images, time, and graphs.
levels: A convolution is like sliding a little stamp across a coloring page, and everywhere the stamp lands it checks whether this little patch looks like a cat's ear, and writes down the answer.

A convolution slides a small filter, a little grid of numbers, across a bigger grid, like an image, and, at every position, multiplies the overlapping numbers together and adds them up. That single filter can then spot the same pattern, an edge, a curve, anywhere it appears in the image. Stacking many filters and layers lets a network build up from simple patterns to complicated ones, like a whole face.

A 2-D convolution slides, say, a 3×3 filter across every position of an image, computing one weighted sum per position, so a single filter with the right weights finds one pattern, like a vertical edge, wherever it occurs, instead of needing a separate detector for every location. A 1-D convolution does the same thing over time instead of over two spatial dimensions, sliding a filter across a sequence of readings, which is how temporal convolutions look for short-term patterns in a time series like a station's speed history. Key knobs are stride, how far the filter moves each step, and padding, whether the edges are filled in so the output stays the same size; stacking convolution layers with pooling in between, which shrinks the image, is the core recipe of a convolutional neural network.

Convolution's two big advantages, weight sharing, the same filter's weights are reused at every position, and locality, each output value depends only on a small neighborhood of the input, make it far more data-efficient than a fully connected layer for grid-structured data, and give it translation equivariance: shifting the input shifts the output the same way, so the network does not need to relearn a pattern separately at every image location. The idea generalizes past images and plain 1-D sequences in this course's own domain: spectral graph convolution, used in STGCN, generalizes convolution to a graph by working in the eigenbasis of the graph Laplacian, approximated efficiently with Chebyshev polynomial filters, while diffusion convolution, used in DCRNN, instead directly applies powers of a random-walk transition matrix, treating message-passing on the road graph as a form of convolution defined by graph structure rather than a Euclidean grid. Both graph variants inherit convolution's core motivation, share weights, exploit local or K-hop structure, but adapt it because a road network has no natural fixed grid the way an image does.

A subtlety that separates naive from sophisticated use of convolution is understanding it as a specific linear operator with structure, mathematically a Toeplitz matrix multiplication, which is why depthwise separable convolutions, factoring a full convolution into a cheaper per-channel step plus a 1×1 mixing step, can approximate a full convolution's expressiveness at a fraction of the compute, a tradeoff that matters enormously for on-device deployment. On graphs specifically, practitioners often assume spectral graph convolution and diffusion convolution are interchangeable graph convolution, but they encode different structural assumptions, spectral methods implicitly assume an undirected graph, while diffusion convolution naturally handles the directed structure of a road network, which is a real reason to prefer one over the other for a directed freeway graph rather than a purely stylistic choice. Residual, or skip, connections, now standard alongside convolutional stacks in both vision and graph networks, exist specifically to fix an optimization pathology, very deep stacks of convolutions become hard to train without them, not to add representational power the plain stack lacked.

At production and research scale, plain 2-D convolution's dominance in vision has been increasingly challenged by attention-based architectures, though convolutions remain the efficient default for on-device and latency-constrained deployment because of their strong inductive bias and comparatively cheap compute per parameter, a real consideration for anything running locally rather than in a data center. In the spatio-temporal domain this course's project touches, the open research question is less convolution versus not and more which structural assumption, a fixed geographic graph convolution, a learned diffusion process, or a fully adaptive, learned adjacency, generalizes best to road networks and traffic patterns the model was not trained on, since a filter's usefulness for images has a much less settled analogue for what a good local pattern means on an arbitrary road graph.

gcn.def: Graph neural networks for traffic: GCN mixes each station with its neighbors, STGCN adds temporal convolutions, DCRNN adds directional diffusion and a sequence model.
levels: These are computer brains that let each road-watcher on a map whisper to its next-door neighbors, share what they are seeing, and pass the news along the road.

A GCN, graph convolutional network, is a neural network built for data that lives on a graph, like stations connected to their neighbors on a freeway, where each station updates its own summary by mixing in its neighbors' summaries. STGCN and DCRNN are two specific designs built for traffic: STGCN alternates looking at time patterns and looking at neighbor patterns, while DCRNN combines a GRU, good at sequences, with a version of neighbor-mixing that respects the one-way direction of traffic flow.

A GCN updates each node's, or station's, representation using its neighbors, via something like `A @ h`, mixing in neighbor information, then a learned weight matrix and nonlinearity, stacked in layers so information can reach further neighbors with each added layer. STGCN alternates gated temporal convolutions, which look for patterns across recent time steps, with Chebyshev graph convolutions, a spectral form of graph convolution, so it captures both when and where patterns. DCRNN instead uses diffusion convolution, applying forward and backward random-walk matrices on the directed road graph, wrapped inside an encoder-decoder GRU that reads a sequence of past readings and predicts a sequence of future ones, with scheduled sampling to make training match how it is actually used at prediction time.

All three are ways of combining two things a plain sequence model or a plain per-station model lacks together: spatial structure, what affects what given the road graph, and temporal structure, how a station's own history predicts its near future. GCN alone provides only the spatial half, mixing each node with its graph neighbors through learned weight matrices, typically requiring full-batch access to the whole graph during training, which is what makes it hard to scale to very large graphs without neighbor-sampling extensions like GraphSAGE. STGCN and DCRNN each combine spatial and temporal modeling but with different design choices, reflecting different assumptions about the road network: STGCN's spectral graph convolution implicitly assumes something close to an undirected graph, while DCRNN's diffusion convolution explicitly models forward and backward random walks on a directed graph, arguably a better structural match for one-way traffic flow, at the cost of a more complex encoder-decoder training procedure with scheduled sampling to bridge the gap between training and inference.

A subtlety practitioners often get wrong when reading this literature is treating graph neural network for traffic as one interchangeable technique, when the design choices, symmetric versus directed adjacency, spectral versus spatial convolution, joint sequence prediction versus per-horizon classification, are not incidental implementation details but encode different, sometimes incompatible, assumptions about how traffic actually propagates. This course's own challenger model, a shared GRU plus two rounds of neighbor mixing with directed A_up and A_down matrices, is explicitly described as a stripped-down DCRNN, illustrating that the real architectures in the literature are often elaborations of a much simpler core idea, sequence model plus K-hop directed message passing, rather than something categorically different. Benchmarks report MAE, RMSE, and MAPE at 15, 30, and 60 minutes on standard datasets, METR-LA, PEMS-BAY, and comparing a reproduction's numbers against a paper's published table, as this course's reading-and-reproducing phase does, routinely surfaces both implementation subtleties and genuine gaps between what a paper reports and what a careful from-scratch reproduction actually achieves.

At the scale of a full metro or state highway network rather than one corridor, full-batch GCN-style training becomes infeasible, and production and research systems adopt neighbor sampling, GraphSAGE, subgraph sampling, Cluster-GCN, or precomputed propagation, SGC, to make training tractable on graphs with tens of thousands of nodes. Open questions this course flags as thesis-chapter-worthy remain genuinely open in the field: multi-horizon coherence, making sure a model's 15, 30, and 60-minute predictions relate sensibly to each other, handling non-stationarity, whether the model adapts online or gets periodically retrained, and performative prediction, the fact that drivers who see and react to a traffic alert change the very future the model was trying to predict, a feedback loop that graph-based traffic forecasting research has only recently started to treat seriously.

roc.def: A curve plotting true-positive rate against false-positive rate as the threshold moves; its area (AUC) summarizes ranking quality but looks flattering under imbalance.
levels: Imagine trying every possible worry-level for ringing an alarm bell, from always ring it to never ring it, and drawing a picture of how often you are right versus wrong at each setting. That picture is the ROC curve.

ROC stands for receiver operating characteristic, a curve that plots how many real positives you catch against how many false alarms you raise, as you slide the alert threshold from very cautious to very trigger-happy. AUC, area under the curve, is a single number, between 0.5, no better than guessing, and 1.0, perfect, summarizing that whole curve into one score. ROC-AUC is a common way to grade a classifier, alongside precision, recall, and F1.

The ROC curve plots the true positive rate, recall, on one axis against the false positive rate on the other, at every possible threshold, so it traces how the tradeoff between catching real positives and raising false alarms changes as the threshold moves. AUC, the area under that curve, is a single summary score between 0.5 and 1.0 that does not require picking any one threshold, and it has a clean interpretation: it equals the probability that a randomly chosen positive example gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one. In this course, scikit-learn's tools compute ROC-AUC alongside the precision-recall curve and average precision, but average precision, not ROC-AUC, is treated as the headline metric.

ROC-AUC's key mathematical property, that it depends only on the relative ranking of scores, not the actual predicted probabilities, and is computed from rates rather than counts, is exactly what makes it look deceptively good under severe class imbalance: because true negatives vastly outnumber positives in an imbalanced problem like slow-traffic prediction, with a five percent positive rate, the false positive rate stays low even when a model makes many false alarms in absolute count, since those false alarms are a small fraction of the huge negative population. The precision-recall curve and its area, average precision, instead directly track precision, what fraction of alarms are correct, which does not get inflated by a huge negative class the way the false positive rate does, which is why this course prefers average precision as the metric that actually reflects operational usefulness for a rare-event alerting problem. ROC-AUC remains useful and standard in balanced or moderately imbalanced problems, and as a ranking-quality check independent of any particular threshold, but reporting it alone on a severely imbalanced problem without also reporting precision-recall metrics risks a misleadingly rosy picture.

A subtlety practitioners frequently get wrong is treating ROC-AUC as a threshold-free, always-appropriate summary simply because it is standard, without asking whether the two error types it balances actually reflect the real operational cost structure; for an alerting system where false alarms directly cost trust while missed jams cost something different, a metric built around the actual decision, precision at a required recall, is more honest than a threshold-free ranking summary that never confronts the actual operating point that will be deployed. There is also a statistical subtlety: ROC-AUC has a known, elegant nonparametric interpretation, the Mann-Whitney U statistic, that makes it attractive for comparing models' ranking ability in a way that is somewhat robust to class balance shifts between training and deployment, a property average precision does not share as cleanly, since AP's absolute value is itself sensitive to the positive rate. Reporting both, ROC-AUC for a class-balance-robust ranking check and average precision for an operationally meaningful summary under the true imbalance, rather than picking one, is the practice more careful teams follow, even though this course deliberately emphasizes only average precision as its headline number.

In production systems facing severe class imbalance, fraud detection, rare medical events, rare traffic incidents, ROC-AUC is often reported alongside precision-recall metrics specifically because stakeholders unfamiliar with the imbalance pitfall default to asking for the AUC, and a model comparison based on ROC-AUC alone can rank two models in the opposite order from what precision-recall-based metrics would show, a discrepancy worth surfacing explicitly rather than silently picking whichever metric favors the preferred model. An open measurement question at scale is how to make ROC-AUC and precision-recall-based comparisons robust to positive-rate drift between training, validation, and live deployment, since a model's AUC can look stable while its live precision at a fixed threshold degrades sharply if the true prevalence of positives shifts after deployment, exactly the kind of silent metric-versus-reality gap a monitoring system built only around AUC would miss.

feature-store.def: Infrastructure that computes and serves the same feature values to both training and live prediction, keeping them consistent and correct as of each moment in time.
levels: A feature store is like a shared recipe box that both the kitchen practicing a dish and the kitchen actually serving dinner use, so the food tastes the same both times.

A feature store is a piece of infrastructure that computes input columns, features, once and serves them consistently to two different places: the pipeline that trains a model, and the live system that makes predictions. Without one, a team risks computing a feature slightly differently in each place, which can quietly break a model that worked fine in testing. Big companies build feature stores; this project's small-scale answer is simpler, one shared piece of code used by both paths.

A feature store solves point-in-time correctness: making sure a training example's features are computed exactly as they would have been known at that moment, no peeking at future data, while a live serving system also needs those same features computed instantly from current data. It typically has two backing stores, an offline data warehouse for building large historical training sets and an online key-value store for fast lookups at prediction time, and a time-travel join that can reconstruct what a feature's value was at any past moment. This project does not use a real feature store; instead, one feature module is imported by both the training script and the prediction script, plus a golden-file test comparing their outputs bit for bit, achieving the same consistency goal at a much smaller scale.

The central problem a feature store solves, offline and online skew, arises because training pipelines typically compute features in batch over historical data, fast, can look at a whole table at once, while serving pipelines compute or fetch features under tight latency constraints from live, incomplete data, and any difference between how a feature is defined or computed in the two paths, even a subtly different rolling-window boundary, produces a model that performs well offline and poorly once deployed. Time-travel joins are the mechanism a feature store uses to guarantee point-in-time correctness at training time: rather than joining a label to whatever the current feature value happens to be, the join reconstructs the feature's value as of the label's own timestamp, which requires storing feature history, not just the latest value, in the offline warehouse. This project's approach, one Python module computing features that both a batch training script and a live prediction script import, sidesteps most of this complexity because both paths run the same code rather than two independently maintained pipelines, a reasonable simplification at the scale of one Mac mini but one that does not remove the underlying correctness requirement, only makes it cheaper to satisfy by sharing code instead of building infrastructure.

A subtlety practitioners commonly get wrong even with a real feature store in place is assuming that using the same feature store automatically guarantees consistency, when the online and offline stores are still often separate systems that must be kept synchronized, and a lag or bug in that synchronization reintroduces exactly the skew the feature store was meant to prevent, just one layer further down. Feature stores also introduce governance and versioning obligations that are easy to underweight until they cause an incident: features change definition over time, and without careful versioning, a model trained against one feature definition can silently start receiving a different one in production, degrading performance in a way that looks like drift but is actually a feature-pipeline change. There is a real cost-benefit judgment to make about whether a feature store is worth building at all: for a small team or a single-machine project, the operational overhead of running and maintaining offline and online consistency infrastructure can exceed the value it provides, which is exactly the argument for this course's minimal shared-module approach over adopting a full feature-store framework prematurely.

At the scale where many models across a company share overlapping features, a feature store's value shifts from preventing training and serving skew for one model to preventing redundant, inconsistent feature computation across many teams, since without shared infrastructure, ten teams computing a rolling 7-day average ten slightly different ways is both wasteful and a source of silent inconsistency across a company's models. The open engineering problems at that scale are less about the basic online and offline consistency this course's small example already achieves and more about governance at organizational scale: lineage, which models depend on which feature, access control over sensitive features, and reconciling a warehouse that is constantly being backfilled or corrected with training sets built from an earlier, now-stale version of that same warehouse.

sql.def: The language for asking a database questions: SELECT picks columns, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY aggregates by group, ORDER BY sorts, JOIN combines tables.
levels: SQL is how you ask a big filing cabinet of information a question out loud, like show me every red toy, biggest first, and it hands you back exactly that.

SQL is a language for asking questions of a database, a place that stores tables of rows and columns. `SELECT` picks which columns you want to see, `WHERE` filters which rows, `GROUP BY` groups rows together to count or average within each group, and `ORDER BY` sorts the results. For example, `SELECT road_names, COUNT(*) FROM events GROUP BY road_names ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC` shows which roads had the most incidents, most first.

A basic SQL query has a fixed shape: `SELECT` names the columns, or an aggregate like `COUNT(*)`, `FROM` names the table, `WHERE` filters rows before any grouping happens, `GROUP BY` collapses rows sharing a value into one row per group so an aggregate can be computed per group, and `ORDER BY` sorts the final result; `JOIN` combines two tables that share a key, like incidents and stations. Running `SELECT road_names, COUNT(*) AS n FROM events GROUP BY road_names ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 5` against the incident log, in DuckDB or SQLite, answers which five roads had the most reported events without writing any pandas code. `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation, unlike `WHERE`, which filters rows before, and window functions like `LAG` or `AVG() OVER` compute a lag or rolling average inside the database, the same thing `.shift()` and `.rolling()` do in pandas.

SQL's declarative nature, you describe what result you want, not the step-by-step procedure to get it, means a query optimizer, not the programmer, decides how to execute a query: which table to scan first, whether to use an index, how to order a join, and understanding that separation, reading an `EXPLAIN` plan to see the chosen execution strategy, is what separates writing correct SQL from writing fast SQL. DuckDB specifically is built for analytical queries over columnar data and can query Parquet files directly without a separate load step, making it a strong fit for this project's cleaned traffic data, whereas SQLite, a single-file database with no server, suits smaller, transactional workloads better. A feature pipeline written entirely in SQL over Parquet, rather than in pandas, is often both faster, the query engine can push filters down before reading unnecessary data, and easier to audit, since the SQL itself is a readable specification of exactly what was computed, but SQL is comparatively awkward for anything requiring row-by-row Python logic or calling out to a machine learning library mid-computation.

A subtlety that separates competent from expert SQL use is understanding why some operations are cheap and others are not from a query plan: an index accelerates targeted lookups but does nothing for a full table scan or a `GROUP BY` over most of the table, and predicate pushdown, filtering before rather than after a join or aggregation, can change a query's runtime by orders of magnitude even though two differently-written queries return identical results. Window functions like `LAG` and `AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY station_id ORDER BY timestamp)` deserve particular attention because they let you compute the same lag and rolling-mean features this course builds in pandas directly inside the database, in one query, which becomes the practical choice once data outgrows what comfortably fits in memory as a DataFrame. A common mistake even experienced practitioners make is treating `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` order as if they always commute freely with `WHERE` filtering; because SQL's declarative semantics guarantee the same result regardless of how a query is phrased, but not the same performance, restructuring a slow query to filter earlier or join smaller tables first is a real skill distinct from getting the right answer at all.

At production scale, the same core SQL, `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, window functions, runs largely unchanged across radically different execution engines, a single DuckDB process on one machine, a distributed engine like Spark or BigQuery spanning thousands of machines, which is precisely the argument for writing data transformations in SQL: the same logic scales from a laptop prototype to a production pipeline with mostly the same code, only the execution engine underneath changes. The remaining engineering complexity at that scale shifts from writing correct queries to query optimization under distribution, predicate pushdown, partition pruning, and join ordering across a cluster, all conceptually the same ideas a single-machine `EXPLAIN` plan already teaches, plus data platform concerns SQL alone does not address: streaming ingestion, table formats supporting time travel, and governance over who can query what, which is where feature stores and data platforms built on top of SQL engines actually earn their complexity.

container.def: A packaged bundle of code, a language runtime, and its libraries that runs identically on any machine; Docker is the standard tool for building and running one.
levels: A container is like a lunchbox packed with everything a helper needs, food, spoon, napkin, so the helper can eat the same lunch no matter whose kitchen they are in.

A container packages a program's code, along with the exact version of Python and libraries it needs, into one bundle that runs the same way on any computer. Docker is the most common tool for building and running containers: a `Dockerfile` lists what goes inside, `docker build` creates the container image, and `docker run` starts it. This solves the works-on-my-machine problem, since the container carries its whole environment with it.

A `Dockerfile` lists a base image, say, a specific Python version, and the install steps needed on top of it, `docker build` turns that recipe into a runnable image, and `docker run` starts a container from that image as an isolated process with its own filesystem and installed packages. A `.dockerignore` file keeps unwanted files, like the `data/` folder, out of the image, the same way `.gitignore` keeps them out of version control. Wrapping a FastAPI prediction endpoint in a container, then running it with `docker run` and calling it with `curl`, is how this course moves a model from runs on my laptop to runs anywhere.

A container differs from a full virtual machine in that it does not virtualize hardware or run a separate operating system kernel; it uses the host operating system's own kernel features, namespaces and cgroups on Linux, to isolate a process's filesystem, network, and resource usage, which is why containers start in milliseconds and use far less overhead than a VM, at the cost of somewhat weaker isolation guarantees. This makes containers well suited to packaging and shipping an application's exact dependency set so that works on my machine becomes works in this container on any machine with Docker installed, addressing exactly the reproducibility problem a virtual environment addresses for Python packages but extending it to the operating system layer underneath. In a serving context, this project wraps a FastAPI prediction endpoint in a container specifically so it can run consistently whether on a developer's laptop, a different machine, or eventually a cloud virtual machine, decoupling whether the code runs correctly from what machine it is running on.

A subtlety practitioners often underestimate is that a container guarantees dependency reproducibility for the software layer it explicitly captures, Python, pip packages, system libraries listed in the Dockerfile, but not necessarily for everything that affects numerical results, driver versions, GPU libraries, or CPU instruction sets outside the container's control can still cause a model to behave slightly differently across machines, which is why ML-specific reproducibility often needs more than a plain application container, pinned CUDA and driver versions, or a hermetic build system like Nix or Bazel for the truly demanding cases. Image size and build caching are practical concerns that separate a well-built Dockerfile from a poorly built one: ordering instructions so that rarely-changing steps come before frequently-changing ones lets Docker's layer cache avoid rebuilding the expensive parts on every small code change, a discipline that matters a great deal once containers are rebuilt many times a day in a CI pipeline. Containers versus orchestration is also a distinction worth being precise about: a single `docker run` is fine for one service on one machine, but running many containers reliably, restarting failed ones, load-balancing across replicas, requires an orchestrator like Kubernetes, a substantially larger and more complex system that this project's single-Mac deployment deliberately does not need.

At production scale, containers are the standard unit of deployment precisely because they let infrastructure teams treat what runs as an immutable, versioned artifact independent of the underlying fleet of machines, enabling patterns like canary releases and rollback that this project's single-machine deployment does not need but that any team serving traffic at real scale relies on constantly. The deeper reproducibility problem containers only partially solve, and hermetic build systems like Nix and Bazel try to solve more completely, is that a container's base image and package installs are themselves fetched from mutable, external sources at build time unless pinned with extreme care, so the same Dockerfile built six months apart can silently produce a different image, exactly the kind of reproducibility failure that makes ML research results hard to check a year later without a much stricter build discipline than most application containers bother with.

y-30.def: The training label: whether a station will be inside a slow episode 30 minutes from now, made by shifting the `label` column six rows earlier.
levels: `y_30` is a peek into the future glued onto today's row: it says yes or no to whether the road will be slow half an hour from right now.

`y_30` is the target column the model tries to predict: whether a station will be in a slow episode 30 minutes after the current row's timestamp. It is built with `s["y_30"] = s["label"].shift(-6)`, taking the slow-or-not label from six rows later, each row is five minutes, so six rows is thirty minutes, and attaching it to the current row. This is the only kind of column in the whole table allowed to look into the future.

`y_30` is made by shifting the `label` column back by six rows within each station's own time series: `s["y_30"] = s["label"].shift(-6)`. The check that this worked is comparing two specific rows: `s.loc[100, ["timestamp", "speed_lag_0", "y_30"]]` printed alongside `s.loc[106, ["timestamp", "label"]]` should show the same value for `y_30` at row 100 and `label` at row 106, with timestamps exactly thirty minutes apart. `s["y_30"].mean()` gives the prevalence, the fraction of rows that are positive, which also happens to be the average precision a random guesser would score.

`y_30` sits alongside `y_15` and `y_60` as the three horizon-specific targets this course builds, each made the same way, a negative shift of the `label` column by 3, 6, or 12 rows respectively, and each defining a separate supervised classification problem: predict whether the station is inside a slow episode that many minutes from now, using only information available up to the current row. Because `y_30` looks forward, `train_table = df.dropna(subset=["y_15", "y_30", "y_60"])` drops the last hour of every station's data, where the future rows needed to compute the labels do not exist yet, and any feature accidentally including future information, rather than only `y_30` itself, is a leakage bug, not a legitimate feature. Correlation between `speed_lag_0` and `y_30` is expected to be weaker than with `y_15` but stronger than with `y_60`, since momentum decays in predictive power the further out the target horizon reaches, a useful sanity check before any model is trained.

A subtlety with `y_30`, and its sibling horizons, that practitioners get wrong is treating three separately-trained classifiers, one per horizon, as if their outputs are automatically coherent, when nothing in the direct multi-horizon setup forces the 15, 30, and 60-minute probabilities for the same row to relate sensibly, a model could in principle predict a higher probability of slow traffic at 15 minutes than at 30 minutes for the same row, which is logically odd if the 30-minute label subsumes the 15-minute one's information. `y_30`'s definition as inside a slow episode rather than speed crosses a threshold also matters: because a slow episode requires three consecutive five-minute steps below the station's typical speed, `y_30` is somewhat robust to a single noisy reading, but it also means a borderline case produces a negative label even though the traffic genuinely was bad, a labeling choice worth understanding rather than treating `y_30` as ground truth beyond dispute. The persistence and profile-rate baselines this course computes against `y_30` exist specifically so that a trained model's score is judged against how much better it does than trivial guesses, not in isolation.

At production scale, a fixed 30-minute horizon target like `y_30` is a specific, somewhat arbitrary operating point chosen for a particular alerting product; research and production systems increasingly move toward joint or continuous-horizon prediction, a single model outputting a full distribution or curve over horizons rather than three independently-trained binary classifiers, specifically to fix the incoherence problem where `y_15`, `y_30`, and `y_60` predictions can otherwise contradict each other. The open modeling question `y_30`'s simple binary framing sidesteps is whether a richer target, regressing the actual speed ratio with a pinball loss, or modeling slow-episode onset as a point process with a hazard rate, captures more of the real signal than a fixed threshold-and-horizon binary label does, at the cost of a harder-to-explain, harder-to-calibrate output than a single number between 0 and 1.

nn-module.def: PyTorch's base class for a model piece: `forward` computes the output from the input, and `backward` (via autograd) computes every gradient automatically.
levels: `nn.Module` is like a recipe card for a piece of a robot's brain: the `forward` part says how it turns ingredients into a dish, and `backward` is how it figures out, after tasting, what to change next time.

`nn.Module` is the basic building block PyTorch uses for any piece of a neural network. When you write a class based on it, `__init__` sets up the learnable parts, like layers with weights, and `forward` describes how input becomes output by using those parts. PyTorch automatically figures out `backward`, how each weight should change to reduce error, using a technique called autograd, so you rarely write backward-pass math by hand.

A model piece written as `class Mix(nn.Module):` defines its learnable parts inside `__init__`, for example two linear layers, and its computation inside `forward`, which says exactly how an input tensor turns into an output tensor. During training, the loop runs `opt.zero_grad()` to clear old gradients, calls the model, which runs `forward`, computes the loss, then calls `.backward()`, which walks the computation backward through every operation `forward` did and fills in the gradient of every parameter, and finally `opt.step()` updates the weights using those gradients. `net.train()` and `net.eval()` switch the model between training and evaluation modes, which matters for certain layers even though it makes no difference for a model this simple.

`nn.Module` is PyTorch's abstraction for composability: any module, a single linear layer or an entire multi-layer network, exposes the same interface, parameters, a `forward` method, which is what lets modules be nested arbitrarily inside larger modules and trained with the same generic training loop regardless of internal complexity. `backward()` is not hand-written per model; it is reverse-mode automatic differentiation applied to whatever computational graph `forward` built during that specific call, which is why changing `forward`'s logic automatically changes what `backward()` computes, with no separate gradient code to keep in sync. `torch.no_grad()` disables this graph-building and gradient bookkeeping for code, like evaluation, that does not need gradients, which both saves memory and prevents accidentally computing gradients through code that should not affect training. A residual connection, writing `forward` so the output includes the input added back in, is a small but important design pattern this course's own graph-mixing module uses, letting a layer's output default to its input if the learned transformation turns out not to help.

The mechanics `nn.Module` and `.backward()` hide from a user, building and traversing a dynamic computational graph, are exactly what earlier logistic regression and MLP lessons in this course derive by hand, and understanding that hand-derived version first is what makes autograd legible rather than magical: `.backward()` is doing the same chain-rule bookkeeping as the manual `backward` function, just generalized to an arbitrary graph of operations rather than one fixed architecture. A subtlety that trips up practitioners moving from hand-written gradients to autograd is forgetting `opt.zero_grad()`: PyTorch accumulates gradients into `.grad` by default rather than overwriting them, a design choice useful for gradient accumulation across small batches but a common source of silently-wrong training when a fresh gradient is assumed each step. Dynamic graph construction, PyTorch rebuilds the graph on every `forward` call, unlike older static-graph frameworks, is what makes `nn.Module` flexible enough to support data-dependent control flow, useful for models whose structure depends on input, at some runtime cost compared to a graph compiled once ahead of time.

At production and research scale, `nn.Module`'s composability is what lets enormous models, with billions of parameters spread across many custom modules, be built, checkpointed, and distributed across multiple devices while the same forward and autograd-backward contract continues to apply unchanged; the engineering complexity shifts from whether autograd works, a solved problem for standard operations, to efficiently distributing that same automatic differentiation across many GPUs or machines without excessive communication overhead. An open frontier this course's simple graph-mixing `nn.Module` only gestures at is custom, non-standard operations where autograd's generic machinery is too slow or too memory-hungry, hand-written custom `backward` implementations, fused kernels, or gradient checkpointing are increasingly necessary at the scale of the largest research models, meaning the hand-derived-gradient skills this course builds early on remain directly relevant even to teams working well beyond textbook-sized networks.

yield.def: A Python keyword that turns a function into a generator, producing one value at a time instead of building a whole list in memory.
levels: `yield` is like a magician handing you one card at a time from a deck instead of dumping the whole deck in your lap at once.

`yield` is a Python keyword that turns an ordinary function into a generator, a function that hands back one value at a time instead of computing everything up front. Each time you ask for the next value, the function picks up right where it left off. This is useful for reading a huge file: instead of loading the whole thing into memory, a generator can hand you one line at a time.

A function containing `yield` becomes a generator: calling it does not run the function immediately, it returns a generator object, and each `next()` call, or each step of a `for` loop over it, resumes the function until it hits the next `yield`, pausing there and handing back that one value. For example, a generator can read a gzipped PeMS file line by line and `yield` only the lines for Fremont, so the rest of a huge file is never held in memory at once. This is the same streaming pattern `chunksize` provides in pandas, but written by hand for cases pandas's built-in tools do not cover.

A generator's key property is lazy evaluation: nothing inside the function body runs until a value is actually requested, and only one item's worth of work and memory is held at a time, which is what lets a generator process an arbitrarily large file with constant memory, in contrast to building a full list, which requires memory proportional to the whole input. Under the hood, `yield` implements Python's iterator protocol automatically, saving and restoring the function's local state between each resumption, something that would take considerably more code to implement manually with a class. Measuring this in practice, comparing `tracemalloc`'s peak memory reading of a hand-written generator streaming a gzipped file against the memory used reading the whole file into a list at once, is the concrete way this course demonstrates that the difference is not just theoretical.

A subtlety practitioners often miss is that a generator can only be iterated once; once exhausted, it does not reset, so code that assumes it can loop over the same generator twice, the way it could loop over a list twice, fails silently or with a confusing empty-iteration result rather than a clear error, a common source of why did my second pass see nothing bugs. Idempotence, rerunning a streaming pipeline should give the same output, is a real design constraint generators interact with: a generator built on `open(path)` re-runs cleanly from the start each time the outer function is called, but a generator built with hidden mutable state can produce different results depending on prior calls if that state is not carefully scoped, exactly the kind of subtle stateful bug that chunked or streaming pipelines need explicit discipline to avoid. Generators compose well with other generators, a chain of `yield`-based filters, each pulling from the previous lazily, which is a natural way to build a multi-stage streaming pipeline without ever materializing an intermediate full list.

At production scale, the lazy, constant-memory pattern `yield` provides in a single Python process generalizes into stream-processing frameworks, generators chained together, or a true distributed stream processor like Flink, that face the same core tradeoff, process one item at a time with bounded memory versus batch for throughput, just at a scale where a single process's generator is no longer sufficient and the streaming has to be distributed, checkpointed, and made fault-tolerant. The engineering lesson this course's small generator exercise foreshadows is architectural: choosing a streaming design from the start, a generator-based ETL step rather than a function that assumes its whole input fits in memory, is far cheaper than retrofitting streaming into a codebase written under the assumption that data always fits, exactly the kind of decision that determines whether a pipeline built for a 200 MB file still works when the input grows to 200 GB.

linear.def: A quantity computed as a weighted sum of inputs plus a constant, like w·x + b; contrasted with nonlinear functions such as ReLU or the sigmoid.
levels: Something is linear when doubling what you put in doubles what you get out, like pouring twice as much juice into twice as many cups; a linear rule never has any surprise bends in it.

A linear function combines its inputs by multiplying each one by a weight and adding the results up, plus maybe one extra constant number. In this course, the score behind logistic regression, w·x + b, is linear: it is just weighted clues added together. Linear things are simple and predictable, which makes them a natural starting point before moving to fancier, bendy models.

A linear function of several inputs x₁, x₂, … has the form w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + … + b, a weighted sum plus a constant, written compactly as w·x + b using the dot product. Geometrically, the set of points where w·x + b = 0 is a straight line, or with more dimensions a flat plane, which is why this is called a linear decision boundary in logistic regression, before the sigmoid bends it into a probability curve. Linear regression itself, y ≈ w·x + b fit by minimizing squared error, is the plainest example: change any one input by 1 unit and the prediction changes by exactly that input's weight, no matter what the other inputs are.

A function is linear in the strict mathematical sense if it satisfies f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) and f(cx) = c·f(x); w·x on its own is linear in this sense, while adding the bias b makes w·x + b technically affine, though linear model is used loosely in machine learning to mean this affine form throughout. Linearity is what makes a model's output change proportionally and predictably as an input changes, which is both linear regression's main strength, interpretable coefficients, one weight per feature, and its main limitation, since it cannot represent an interaction, where one feature's effect on the target depends on another feature's value, without those interactions being explicitly added as extra features. Nonlinearity is introduced deliberately wherever a model needs to bend, the sigmoid squashes a linear score into a valid probability, ReLU lets a neural network's hidden layers represent curved decision boundaries that a purely linear stack of layers could never produce, since stacking multiple linear layers with no nonlinearity between them collapses mathematically into a single linear layer.

A subtlety worth being precise about is that linear in the parameters and linear in the inputs are different properties that get conflated: polynomial regression, fitting y ≈ w₁x + w₂x² + b, is nonlinear in x but still linear in the weights w₁, w₂, which is why it can still be fit by the same least-squares machinery as ordinary linear regression, just with x² added as an extra engineered feature, a distinction that matters for understanding why linear model does not mean cannot capture curved relationships at all. Deep networks fail to reduce to a single linear layer specifically because a nonlinearity is inserted between every pair of linear layers; without it, W₂(W₁x) is just a single linear transformation, no matter how many layers are stacked, which is the precise mathematical reason depth only buys expressive power when nonlinear activations are present. A practitioner mistake worth flagging: assuming a linear model's coefficients directly reflect causal importance, when correlated features split a linear model's weight between them in ways that make individual coefficients misleading without also checking multicollinearity, much as gain-based feature importance is misleading for correlated features in a tree model.

At production and research scale, linearity remains foundational even in deep systems built almost entirely from nonlinear components: the linear, matrix multiplication, operations are what dominate compute cost and what specialized hardware, matrix multiply units, tensor cores, is built to accelerate, so understanding exactly which parts of a model are linear algebra kernels versus nonlinear activations is directly relevant to why some architectural choices are fast and others are not on real hardware. Linear models also persist as the calibration, baseline, and interpretability layer even inside heavily nonlinear production systems, a linear probe on top of a deep network's learned features, a linear calibration step applied to an otherwise nonlinear model's output, precisely because linearity's predictability and interpretability remain valuable even after a nonlinear model has done the harder representational work.
